issues.legal_issue: Eviction for demolition and reconstruction requires a genuine, direct and timely need supported by the condition of the existing building and the circumstances as a whole.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction to demolish the existing building and erect a new one, partly to put the property to better use.
The Rent Controller found the building structurally safe and sound but treated its condition as irrelevant to whether the landlord had a bona fide requirement.
The appellate authority and the High Court affirmed the eviction order despite the building's sound condition.
issues.conclusion: The building's condition is an essential requirement for eviction for demolition and reconstruction. It need not be on the verge of collapse, but it must warrant timely demolition; a sound and safe building does not qualify. Because the authorities disregarded the building's sound condition, eviction could not be ordered in this case.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(1)(b) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 requires a bona fide, direct and timely purpose of demolishing the existing building to erect a new one. The building's condition must make demolition appropriate, such as where repair would be uneconomical or the building unsafe; the condition need not be so grave that collapse is imminent. The authority must also consider the totality of relevant circumstances, including the landlord's capacity to rebuild, the locality, demand for accommodation and advantages of reconstruction. Personal residential or business need is not germane to section 14(1)(b), and cannot be imported from section 10. The construction must serve the Act's stated object of controlling rents and preventing unreasonable eviction. The Court relied on Metalware & Co. v. Bansilal Sarma & Co. and Neta Ram v. Jiwan Lal; approved Mehsin Bhai v. Hale & Company G.T., K. Ramachandra Rao v. Krishnaswami Iyengar and K.P. Lonaopan and Sons v. S. Mohamed Iqbal; distinguished Panchamal Narayan Shenoy v. Basthi Venkatesha Shenoy; and relied on Prabhakaran Nair v. State of Tamil Nadu concerning the Act's legislative object.

rule.if: demolition_eviction_case and building_condition_requires_timely_demolition and direct_timely_reconstruction_purpose and total_circumstances_support_bona_fides

predicates.demolition_eviction_case: A landlord seeks eviction of a tenant so the existing building can be demolished and a new building erected.
predicates.building_condition_requires_timely_demol: The existing building's condition makes timely demolition appropriate, such as because repair would be uneconomical or the building unsafe.
predicates.direct_timely_reconstruction_purpose: The landlord's genuine purpose is directly connected to demolishing the existing building and erecting a new one, without undue or protracted delay.
predicates.total_circumstances_support_bona_fides: The relevant circumstances, including the landlord's capacity to rebuild and the circumstances of the property and locality, support the genuineness of the proposed reconstruction.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks demolition-based eviction, the rule permits eviction only if the building's condition warrants timely demolition, the reconstruction purpose is direct and timely, and the circumstances support the landlord's bona fides.

issues.legal_issue: A court exercising judicial review may reverse an eviction finding when the competent authority applies the wrong legal test or disregards relevant circumstances.
material_facts: The Rent Controller considered the building's condition irrelevant and disregarded the landlord's admission and other evidence that the building was sound.
The appellate authority and the High Court affirmed the eviction order.
The Supreme Court held that the authorities had asked themselves the wrong question and had failed to apply the essential requirement concerning the building's condition.
issues.conclusion: The authorities' findings were liable to be reversed because they misapplied the law and failed to consider a relevant and essential circumstance; the appeal was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: In judicial review, a court does not ordinarily reappreciate evidence or substitute its view for that of the authority empowered to decide facts. The authority's decision is generally final if it considers relevant facts, excludes irrelevant matters, applies the law correctly and observes natural justice. Its conclusions may be reversed if it exceeds its jurisdiction, asks the wrong question, misunderstands or misapplies the law, or fails to consider relevant circumstances. Here, the authorities treated the building's condition as irrelevant despite evidence that it was sound, and therefore applied the wrong test.

predicates.judicial_review_of_rent_eviction_finding: A court reviews a competent authority's factual finding in a rent-control eviction proceeding.
predicates.authority_misapplied_law_or_ignored_rele: The authority applied an incorrect legal test or failed to consider relevant evidence or circumstances.

issues.definition: In judicial review of a rent-control eviction finding, a finding is open to reversal when the authority applied the wrong law or ignored relevant facts.
